Header:
Date: 2026-06-18

Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Ortega (Redwood SE), Elena Park (CTO, Ember), Ramesh Patel (Head of ML), Clara James (Eng Manager), Jordan Lee (DevOps)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Redwood demo of hosted API features focusing on chat/text generation basics incl streaming, param tuning, retry logic. Customer asks about latency/cost tradeoffs and compliance. Next steps captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everybody, thanks for joining um we'll wait one min for folks to pop in.
[00:12] Elena: Yep thanks Maya, I'm here. Ramesh and Clara are on as well.
[00:18] Maya: Great. Quick round-robin, I'm Maya Chen, AE, and Lucas Ortega is our SE, he'll do most of the demo.
[00:26] Lucas: Hi team quick agenda: streaming responses, parameters like temperature/top_p/max_tokens, retry behavior and idempotency, and how you can see fast traces in the Console.
[00:38] Ramesh: Sounds good. We mostly care about throughput and tail latency we run chat agents for commerce flows and need sub-300ms p50 ideally for short prompts.
[00:47] Lucas: Got it. Two quick clarifications when you say sub-300ms, is that token-latency or end-to-end response for a few hundred token outputs?
[00:55] Ramesh: End-to-end for ~40 token responses.
[01:02] Lucas: Cool. We'll show streaming which helps perceived latency for the UI, and batching/caching/options that Redwood has under the hood.
[01:12] Elena: Also send over your SOC 2 & security docs, and details on data retention.
[01:19] Maya: Absolutely we'll put the security pack link in chat after.

[01:35] Lucas: Kicking off the demo here's the Hosted API playground. Example request: model=redwood-2-small, mode=chat, messages array, and we set stream=true for chunked tokens.
[01:50] Lucas: When stream=true you get SSE chunks as tokens are generated front-ends can render progressively so users feel immediate response even if final tokens take longer.
[02:05] Clara: Is the stream over HTTP/1.1 or do you support ws/sse?
[02:10] Lucas: We support server-sent events and chunked HTTP, not full websockets for streaming right now. Some customers build a thin websocket gateway.
[02:23] Jordan: Any issues with intermediate chunks being dropped under heavy load?
[02:28] Lucas: We have retries at the chunk level in our client libs and the server supports graceful reconnect with resume tokens/KV-cache pointers; though sometimes the transcripting here I'm sure says KV cash or k-v cache it's the KV cache for autoregressive state.
[02:45] Ramesh: Right, resume is key for mobile.

[03:00] Lucas: Next parameters. Temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling; max_tokens limits output length. We showed a demo toggling temperature 0.0, 0.7, 1.0 and you can see output diversity change.
[03:20] Lucas: Also surface-level param: stop sequences/stop_tokens and presence_penalty/frequency_penalty for biasing.
[03:30] Elena: For safety, do you have automatic content filters or do we run filters client-side?
[03:36] Lucas: Redwood offers optional moderation hooks that run prior to returning responses for hosted customers, and you can chain your own filters. We'll share the doc.

[04:05] Lucas: Now retries typical failure modes: 5xx server errors, transient timeouts, or rate limit 429s. We recommend an exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency keys on create-like calls. For streaming we suggest client reconnect + resume.
[04:23] Clara: How do idempotency keys work for streaming endpoints?
[04:27] Lucas: You send an idempotency key in the header on the initial request; if you retry the server dedups within the key window. For streaming-specific reconnects, we use the resume token approach.
[04:40] Ramesh: Any guidance on backoff params?
[04:43] Lucas: Example best practice: base=200ms, multiplier=2x, max=10s with jitter. For 429s we add slightly longer windows. We'll include a gist in the follow-up.

[05:10] Maya: On cost side shorter responses and lower temperature help reduce token usage; also Redwood Optimize gives model/quantization recommendations by workload.
[05:22] Elena: Do you expose per-token billing in the Console?
[05:25] Maya: Yes, the Console shows token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards. You can also set quotas and rate limits.

[06:00] Lucas: Quick detour to batching and caching automatic prefix caching and continuous batching can reduce cost but may add latency; you can tune batching window.
[06:12] Jordan: We use Kubernetes and VPC for hosted are you comfortable with our egress rules and IP allowlists?
[06:20] Maya: For hosted we support IP allowlists and private peering in some regions; for strict compliance you can move to Redwood Dedicated or Private.

[06:40] Ramesh: We're considering a hosted pilot first to validate quality. If it looks good we'll talk Dedicated. What's the SLA for hosted?
[06:48] Maya: Hosted has soft uptime targets for enterprise we offer SLA-backed Dedicated. We'll share the SLA doc; hosted is generally high-availability but not the same as Reserved Dedicated.

[07:05] Lucas: I'm going to run a small live example same prompt, stream=true, temperature 0.2. You'll see initial tokens at ~120ms and tail finish at ~250ms in this dev region this is dev lab; production numbers vary.
[07:22] Elena: Looks good on the UI.
[07:28] Lucas: Note that for consistency you can pin a model version, set quantization profiles or serve a lower-capacity variant to trade off latency/cost.

[08:00] Lucas: A little bit of an aside retries and request ids. We emit request id headers and trace ids so you can correlate in your logs and in the Console traces.
[08:12] Clara: Can we stream logs into our SIEM?
[08:15] Lucas: Yes, via webhooks or S3 export for audit logs; Dedicated has richer logging integrations.

[09:00] Elena: About data residency we need EU data stay in EU for PII.
[09:05] Maya: We have region routing and data residency options for Enterprise and Private deployments. Hosted can route by region where available; we'll mark this as a requirement for the pilot.

[09:30] Lucas: Quick note on model selection we maintain a model catalog; for latency-sensitive shorter prompt flows you might pick a smaller verified variant. Optimize can recommend quantization and batching policies.

[10:05] Ramesh: Any caveats on hallucination control?
[10:08] Lucas: Techniques include prompt engineering, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and evals. We have first-class support for embeddings and reranking and built-in eval hooks in the Console.

[12:00] Maya: There's a question in chat about quotas and throttling behaviour during spikes. Our rate limiter is token-based and we expose both soft and hard limits; you can configure burst windows.

[13:20] Jordan: Does Redwood store prompts or are they ephemeral?
[13:25] Lucas: For hosted, by default we may retain minimal logs for troubleshooting; customers can opt-out or request stricter retention and use Private if required. We'll share the retention policy.

[16:00] Lucas: Wrapping the demo we'll summarize: streaming for UX, params for control, retry/backoff/idempotency for reliability, Console for observability, and Optimize for cost/perf tuning.

[16:30] Elena: Thanks some follow-ups on our side: we want pricing for pilot (100k tokens/day), SOC 2 docs, and a benchmark run with our dataset.

[16:40] Maya: Noted. We'll send pricing tiers and pilot options, and Lucas will send the benchmark script.

[17:05] Ramesh: One more thing any built-in client libraries for retries and resume?
[17:10] Lucas: Yes, SDKs for Node/Python have retry helpers, idempotency header helpers, and streaming client utilities. Some methods abstract reconnection and resume token logic I'll link the SDK examples.

[18:00] Clara: Onboarding timeline if pilot looks good, we want to go POC in 3-4 weeks.

[18:06] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll coordinate calendars after this call.

[18:30] Maya: Ok let's do a quick recap of next steps. Lucas you to send benchmark script and sample prompts.
[18:38] Lucas: Yep.
[18:40] Maya: I'll send pricing, SOC 2 and security pack. Ramesh to provide dataset. We'll aim for pilot kickoff the week of 2026-06-29?
[18:51] Ramesh: That works.

[19:00] Elena: Thanks everyone.
[19:05] Maya: Thanks all we'll follow up in email.

[End of recording]
